units.spoken: AlphaZero: Search and Self-Play
A network suggests which lines of play to explore, and the exploring teaches the network.

In the board game Go and chess the rules are known, so the agent can look ahead before each move instead of guessing. A network gives two quick judgements of a position: which moves look promising and what result to expect. A tree search uses those judgements to explore many continuations and counts how often it visited each move. Those visit counts are a better policy than the network's guess; the agent plays that policy against itself. The network is trained to predict the search's choices and the game's result, so next time it guides the search better.

Take a look at this figure. A network suggests moves, the search explores them, and the games the search plays teach the network. The lesson is the loop: the search improves the network, and the network improves the search.

Figure 1 shows the loop that teaches the network. A position goes into the network, which says which moves look good and what result to expect, and the search picks the move from how often each move was tried; the games against itself then train the network on the game result and on those counts. Take one self-play game: its result and its visit shares go back into the network.

sections.section: 1 One quick guess per move misses wins a few moves deep

units.spoken: Section one, One quick guess per move misses wins a few moves deep
Look-ahead
What. Picture a quick guess that misses a win a few moves deep: the agent tries moves in the model, the rules that say what a move leads to, before choosing one for real.
How. Try several moves, then their replies, before choosing one for real.
Why. When it works, the agent finds the win the guess missed.
A program that maps a chess position straight to a move misses a win or a trap that only shows a few moves later.
The running example is chess. In this late position only a few pieces are left, so one good move can decide the game.

Take a look at this figure. A late chess position with only a few pieces left, where one good move can decide the game. The lesson is that a position like this is where looking ahead pays: the win is a few moves deep, and a quick guess misses it.

Figure 2 shows the chess position this page comes back to. The black king sits on a2, the white king on c1 and the white rook on e1, with the black king one step from the corner. Take the rook on e1: it can give check up the file, the column it stands on, or slide up that file to the third rank, the third row up, and Figure 6 shows which the search prefers.
1.1 Agent, state and move

The agent is the learner that picks the moves. A state is the agent's situation right now; a move, or action, is one choice the agent can make in a state; a reward is the number the world hands back after each move, good or bad. Here the agent is a program that plays one side, and the state is the position on the board. Every move turns that position into a new one, so the possible moves branch like a tree.

Two players, called White and Black, take turns, and on each turn the player to move must make exactly one legal move, a move the rules allow. A simple chess program rates the position after each legal move and plays the move whose position rates best.

A policy is the agent's rule for choosing a move in each state; it may always pick the same move or pick by chance. So the quick guesser of the problem above picks its move from the position alone and never looks further.
1.2 The model and the look-ahead

Here a model is anything that tells the agent what a move leads to; for chess that is the rules themselves. A model can be given, like the exact rules of a board game, or learned from the agent's own steps. Chess's model is given in full, so the agent can try moves on it exactly.
Chess players look ahead, and with the rules known the agent can too, but there are far too many possible continuations to try them all.

AlphaZero brings this look ahead to chess, to shogi, which is Japanese chess, and to the board game Go. The same method, with only the rules swapped, learns each game separately, starting from random play.
Dyna-Q's model made training data but never looked ahead at decision time.

sections.section: 2 A network that steers the look-ahead

units.spoken: Section two, A network that steers the look-ahead
The two-head network
What. Picture one look at a position giving both which moves look good and what result to expect.
How. One output branch, the policy head, gives a chance per legal move, and a second branch, the value head, estimates the result.
Why. When it works, the search tries the promising branches first and rates a position without playing it out.
In chess no reward arrives until the game ends in a win, a draw or a loss. A single chess game can last many moves on each side.

The return is all the reward still to come, with later rewards counted a little less. Counting later rewards a little less is called a discount. A state's value, V of s, is the return the agent expects from state s. So in Go and chess a position's value is the result the player to move can expect from here. AlphaZero counts the result in full, with no discount, however many moves away it is, so the network must judge positions long before any reward arrives.

A tree search tries moves from the current position, then the replies to them; the current position is the root, and the newest position at the end of a path is a leaf. From any position the tree fans out fast, because every reply opens new branches.
Each node of the tree is a position and each edge is a move. Most paths from the root are never tried, because the tree is far too big.

A head is one output branch of the network. The value head estimates the game result the player to move can expect from here, anywhere from a loss through a draw to a win. The policy head says which branches to try first; the value head rates a position without playing the game out.

Take a look at this figure. One position grows into a tree: each move is a branch, each branch is tried, and the search follows the branches the model likes best. The lesson is that the tree is the search, and the search is what picks the move.

Figure 3 shows a small tree over the chess position. The root is the current position, three moves lead down to the next level, and six leaves sit at the bottom, with crosses marking the branches cut off. Take the leftmost leaf: it sits at the same depth as the others, so the tree stays level even where the search cut branches away.
2.1 Self-play
Self-play
What. Picture the same network playing both sides of the game.
How. Every finished game labels its positions with the result.
Why. When it works, the opponent improves exactly as fast as the player.
An episode is one run from the start until it ends. Here an episode is one game. The game result is a win, a draw or a loss, seen from the player whose turn it is.

Equation 1. The game result. The whole page measures results from the side of the player to move. A game ends in a win, a loss or a draw, and the result is the one number the search carries back from the end of the game to every move that led there.
Take a look at this equation. A game ends in a win, a loss or a draw, and the result is one number that teaches every move that led there.

The result line. Zee is the result of the game, one number. The set in braces holds the three possible results: plus one for a win, zero for a draw, minus one for a loss. The membership sign reads is one of, so zee is one of those three numbers. Intuitively, the result is one number: plus one, zero or minus one.
Intuition. A finished game has only three endings, and every result on this page is read from the side of the player to move.

Example. Take a game that ends in a draw: neither side won, so the result is zero for the player to move. Take a game that ends in checkmate instead: the player to move has lost, so the result is minus one. A win for the player to move is plus one.
So the result of a game is one number, plus one, zero or minus one, and that number is the lesson every move learns from.

sections.section: 3 How the search picks and scores moves

units.spoken: Section three, How the search picks and scores moves
Monte Carlo tree search
What. Picture many simulations, each one pass from the root down to a new leaf and back, counting which moves they went through.
How. Each simulation selects a path down, expands the new leaf, backs its value up, and repeats.
Why. When it works, hundreds of simulations beat one quick guess.
The more simulations the search runs, the deeper and wider the part of the tree it explores.

Monte Carlo means deciding by random trials. The name Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) comes from older searches that played random games to the end. AlphaZero never plays a game out and trusts the value head's guess instead.

A simulator is a program that applies the rules exactly, so a search can step through positions without playing them for real. For chess it is a move generator that knows every rule. The search calls it at every step down the tree, so every position the search reaches is exact.
Equation 2. The network. The search needs quick judgements of every position it reaches, which moves look good and what result to expect. One model, two jobs: suggest moves and judge positions.
Take a look at this equation. One model, two jobs: the policy head suggests moves and the value head judges positions.

The network line. Pee bold is the policy head, the chance of each move. Vee is the value head, the expected result from this position. F sub thay-ta is the network, with weights thay-ta. State s is the position. The round brackets hold the two heads together as one output. Intuitively, the network takes a position and gives back a move suggestion and a value.
Intuition. One look at a position gives both what to try and what to expect.

Example. Take a middlegame position where one move saves a rook the other side could take for free and another loses it: the policy head gives the saving move the higher chance, and the value head gives a value close to a win, since the rook stays on the board.
So one network does two jobs: the policy head suggests moves and the value head judges the position.

The prior is the network's first guess of how good each move is, before any search. The visit count is how many simulations went through a move in a position. Both are stored on every move in the tree.
The search must balance trying rarely tried moves against repeating the ones that look best. A move that looks weak after a few visits can still be the best one.
3.1 Picking the next move
PUCT selection
What. Picture the rule that balances trying rarely tried moves against repeating the best: each move carries a bonus that shrinks as it is tried.
How. Each move's total is its value so far plus its bonus.
Why. When it works, a move the prior likes gets tried early and a move tried often sees its bonus shrink.

The search settles that balance with a rule called PUCT (predictor plus upper confidence bounds, a bonus for moves tried less often, applied to trees). PUCT steers each simulation toward moves that have looked good so far, plus a bonus for moves the prior likes that the search has rarely tried.

A move's value, also called its score, is the return the agent expects if it makes a move in a state and plays on from there. The search keeps that score on every move in the tree, beside the prior and the visit count.
Each simulation picks, at every position on its way down, the move with the best score plus bonus.

Equation 3. The selection rule. The search must balance trying rarely tried moves against repeating the ones that look best. At a position the search must choose: follow the move that has looked best so far, or try a move it has not explored yet.
Take a look at this equation. The search picks the next move by adding a bonus for unexplored moves to the value each move has shown so far.

The bonus line. You is the bonus for trying a move. C sub puct is the weight that sets how much exploring matters. Pee is the network's first guess at this move. The square root on top adds the visits of every move at this position, so it grows with every visit. The bottom grows only for this move, so the bonus shrinks as this move is tried. The plus one keeps the bonus from being zero at a fresh node, so the first visit follows the prior. Intuitively, the bonus is big for moves the network likes and the search has not tried yet.
termList: en of state s and bee
en of state s and action a

units.spoken: Intuition. A move nobody has tried keeps a big bonus, and a move tried often sees its bonus shrink.
Example. Take a move tried often and one never tried: the tried move's bonus has shrunk, and the untried move's bonus is still full.

The choice line. A star is the move the search picks next. Argmax means the move with the largest value. Cue of state s and action a is how good this move has looked so far. Plus adds the bonus, so the search picks the move with the largest value plus bonus. Intuitively, the search picks the move whose value plus bonus is largest.
termList: cue of state s and action a

units.spoken: Intuition. Each move's total is its value so far plus its bonus, and the search follows the biggest total.

Example. Take a position where one move has been tried often and looks good, and another has never been tried: the tried move carries a high value so far and a shrunk bonus, the untried move carries no value yet and a full bonus, so it can still win the step.
So the search picks the next move by value plus bonus: the best move so far wins, unless an untried move the network likes carries a bigger bonus.
The code adds one inside the square root so the first visit follows the prior.

UCT (upper confidence bounds applied to trees) is an older tree-search rule; the form on this card is the variant used in the earlier Go programs AlphaGo and AlphaGo Zero, with the network's move chances as the prior.
3.2 Carrying the value back
Backup
What. Picture a new leaf's value climbing back to the root.
How. Flip the sign at each level, count one more visit, nudge the average one share of the gap to the new value.
Why. When it works, the root's scores carry what the leaf said.

Each simulation ends its way down at a position not yet in the tree. Expanding adds the new leaf to the tree and asks the network about it. The backup carries a new leaf's value back up the path, flipping its sign at each level because the players take turns.

Equation 4. The backup. A simulation ends at a new leaf with one value from the network. That value must travel back up the tree to every move that led there, and the three lines below are the three updates that carry it back.
Take a look at this equation. The value from the end of a line travels back up the tree, and three updates carry it: flip the sign, count the visit, and move the average.

The flip line. Vee gets replaced by minus vee. The value flips sign because the player to move changes at each step up the tree: what is good for one side is bad for the other. Intuitively, the value changes sides as it climbs, so it flips sign at every step.
Intuition. A position good for one side is bad for the other, so the value flips before each edge is credited.
Example. Take a leaf the network values in favour of the player to move there: the value flips as it climbs, so each edge is credited from its own player's side.

The count line. En of state s and action a gets replaced by itself plus one. En is the number of times this move has been tried here, so each visit adds one to the count. Intuitively, the count grows by one every time the search passes through this move.
termList: en of state s and action a

units.spoken: Intuition. Every move on the path counts one more visit.
Example. Take the move on this simulation's path: its count rises by exactly one, and moves off the path are untouched.

The average line. Cue of state s and action a gets replaced by itself plus the gap between the value and itself, divided by the count. Vee is the value carried back from the end of the line. The gap between the value and the old average is the new information, and dividing by the count folds it into the running average. Intuitively, the average moves a little toward each new value, less and less as the count grows.
termList: cue of state s and action a
en of state s and action a

units.spoken: Intuition. Each new value moves the average by one share of the gap, so early values move it more than late ones.

Example. Take a simulation that reaches a new leaf the network values in favour of the player to move there: each move's average moves one share of the gap toward the flipped value, so the scores at the root carry what the leaf said.
So the value travels back up the tree in three updates: flip the sign, count the visit, and move the average toward the new value.
3.3 Learning from the search
The search policy and the loss
What. Picture the search's visits and the game's result teaching the network.
How. Visits become the search policy, and the training loss, the number training makes smaller, pulls the policy head toward those shares and the value head toward the result.
Why. When it works, the next game's guesses start better.

Equation 5. The search policy. The search has run its simulations and the root's visit counts hold what it learned. The visits say which moves were worth trying, and the line below turns those visits into the lesson the model learns from.
Take a look at this equation. The search's visits become the lesson: the move visited most is the move the model learns to prefer.

The search policy line. Pee sub search is the lesson, the chance of each move from the search. En of state s and action a is the number of times the search visited this move. The sum over bee adds the visits of every move at this position. The fraction divides this move's visits by the total, so the visits become chances that add to one. Intuitively, the move visited most gets the largest chance.
termList: en of state s and action a

units.spoken: Intuition. The chance of each move is its share of the root's visits.

Example. Take a root position where the search kept returning to one move and rarely tried the rest: that move holds most of the visits, so its share is most of the search policy, and the search trusts that move.
So the search's visits become the lesson: each move's chance is its share of the visits, and the move visited most is the one the model learns to prefer.
During self-play moves are drawn in proportion to these shares; in a match the most visited move is played.
Cross-entropy is a loss that is lower when the predicted chances put weight where the search's chances put weight. A small extra term pulls every weight toward zero, so no weight grows without need.

Equation 6. The training loss. The search has turned the network's guesses into better move chances, and finished games give true results. The loss also pulls every weight toward zero with an L2 penalty, the squared size of all weights together, keeping the network from memorizing single games. The line below is the whole loss, written as one sum.
Take a look at this equation. The loss has three terms: the value error, the policy error, and a small weight penalty.

The loss line. Ell is the loss, one number that says how wrong the model is. Zee minus vee squared is the value error: the gap between the game's result and the value head's guess. Pee sub search transpose log pee is the policy error: how far the policy head's move chances sit from the search's lesson. C sub L 2 times the size of thay-ta squared is the weight penalty, keeping the weights small. The minus in front of the policy error turns a log chance into a cost. Intuitively, the loss is the value error plus the policy error plus a small weight penalty.
Intuition. Training pulls the network's guesses toward the search's visit shares and the true result.

Example. Take a self-play game White won: every position in it is labelled with that result, a win when White is to move and a loss when Black is, and with the search's visit shares, so the value head learns the result from the side to move and the policy head learns the shares the search gave each move.
So the loss trains both heads at once: the value error, the policy error, and a small weight penalty, added into one number.
Section four, Stepping through one search

Take a look at this walkthrough. It runs one search from the root to the move played and the lesson learned: select a line, expand it, flip the value, back it up, repeat, move, and learn. The lesson is the whole search in one arc: the search explores, the value travels back, and the visits become the lesson.

Try the walkthrough. Press Play to run the search from the root to the move played, or step through it with Next. Watch the search select a line, expand it, flip the value, back it up, and repeat, then move and learn. Press Reset to start over.
Follow one simulation from the root down to a new leaf and back, then the move it picks and what the finished game teaches.
Take a look at this walkthrough. It follows one search through eight steps, and each step lights the line it uses.

The bonus step. The walkthrough reaches the bonus step. You is the bonus for trying a move: c sub puct weights the network's first guess, pee, and the visit ratio shrinks as the move is tried, so an untried move keeps a full bonus.
Intuition. At this step the simulation is still at the root, and the bonus lifts an untried move above a tried one.
Example. Take the root of this search: the untried move's bonus is still full, so the simulation follows it down.

The choice step. The walkthrough reaches the choice step. A star is the move this simulation follows down: the argmax picks the move whose value plus bonus is largest, so a move nobody has tried can still win the step on its bonus alone.
termList: cue of state s and action a

units.spoken: Intuition. Each move's total is its value so far plus its bonus, and the search follows the biggest total.
Example. Take this simulation's step down from the root: it follows the move whose value plus bonus is biggest, not the move with the most visits alone.

The expand step. The walkthrough reaches the expand step. The network reads the new leaf and gives two outputs: the policy head, a chance for each legal move, which becomes the leaf's priors, and the value head, the result to expect from here.
Intuition. The new leaf is a position the network has not judged yet, so one call reads it.
Example. Take the new leaf this simulation reached: one call gives a chance for every legal move and a value for the player to move there.

The flip step. The walkthrough reaches the flip step. Vee is the leaf's value from the side of the player to move there, and the minus turns it into the view of the player who chose the move into the leaf, so each edge is credited from its own player's side.
Intuition. A position good for one side is bad for the other, so the value flips before each edge is credited.
Example. Take the leaf's value: it flips as it climbs, so each edge is credited from its own player's side.
The count step. The walkthrough reaches the count step. En of state s and action a rises by exactly one for each move on the path back to the root, and moves off the path are untouched.
termList: en of state s and action a

units.spoken: Intuition. Every move on the path counts one more visit.
Example. Take each move on the path back: its count rises by exactly one.

The average step. The walkthrough reaches the average step. Cue of state s and action a moves toward the flipped value vee by the gap between them, divided by the new count, so the root's scores carry what the leaf said.
termList: cue of state s and action a
en of state s and action a

units.spoken: Intuition. Each new value moves the average by one share of the gap, so early values move it more than late ones.
Example. Take one edge on the path back: its average moves one share of the gap toward the flipped value.
The move step. The walkthrough reaches the move step. Pee sub search is the chance of each move, its share of the root's visits, so the move the search returned to most is the move played.
termList: en of state s and action a

units.spoken: Intuition. The chance of each move is its share of the root's visits.
Example. Take the root after the simulations: the move the search returned to most holds most of the visits, so its share is most of the search policy.

The learn step. The walkthrough reaches the learn step. Ell is the loss: the value error, the search policy's shares times the log of the policy head's chances, and the L2 penalty, c sub L 2 times the squared size of thay-ta.
Intuition. Training pulls the network's guesses toward the search's visit shares and the true result.
Example. Take the finished game: its result and the root's visit shares teach the network.
So one search runs eight steps: select, expand, flip, back up, repeat, move, and learn, and each round the model and the search make each other better.

Take a look at this figure. One search, eight stages: start at the root, pick a move, ask the network, carry the value back, and learn. The lesson is the loop closing: the search teaches the model, and the model guides the next search.

Figure 4 walks one search through eight stages, from the root down to a new leaf and back, with the network judging the leaf. The stages run: start at the root, follow score plus bonus to a leaf, ask the network, flip the value to the view of the player who chose the move, carry it back counting visits, repeat until visits pile up, play the most visited move, and learn from the game. Take the chess search: the network's move chances become the new leaf's priors, and the leaf's value flips at each level as it climbs back to the root.
Section five, AlphaZero in PyTorch
This section builds the four pieces in code: a two-head network, one PUCT choice, the backup and the loss. The move generator is left out.
5.1 A two-head network

This code builds the network: one body that reads the board, a policy head that suggests moves, and a value head that judges the position. The board comes in as 119 planes of 8 by 8, and the policy head gives a chance for each of the 4672 possible moves.
5.2 One PUCT choice

This code picks the next move: for each move it adds the bonus to the value so far, and it returns the move with the largest sum. The bonus is big for moves the network likes and the search has not tried yet, and illegal moves are masked out before the choice.
5.3 The backup
This code carries the value back up the tree: it flips the sign at each step, adds one to the count, and moves the average toward the new value.
5.4 The policy and the loss

This code turns the search into the lesson and the loss: the visits become the chances the model learns to prefer, and the loss adds the value error and the policy error. The weights are pulled toward zero not by the loss but by the optimizer, with a weight decay of twice C L 2.

These four pieces plug into one training loop. Self-play runs a search at every move, using 5.2 to pick moves down the tree, 5.3 to carry each new value back up, and 5.4 to turn the root's visits into the policy each position is stored with, beside the game's final result. Training then draws 4,096-position batches from the stored games and updates the 5.1 network with the 5.4 loss, and the new network plays the next games.

sections.section: 6 Search finds the winning move the network missed

units.spoken: Section six, Search finds the winning move the network missed
In chess you win by checkmate, which means attacking the opposing king so that it has no safe square left.
White has two pieces left and Black has only one.
A rook slides any distance along its row or its column and attacks every square on them. A king steps one square in any direction and may never step onto a square the other side attacks.
Together they can trap a king against the edge of the board.
White's rook and king stand on the bottom row, and Black's king is near the bottom left corner; White moves first.
A check attacks the king at once, so it looks strong at a glance, and a network that judges at a glance likes it best.

Take a look at this figure. Two moves side by side: the tempting check and the quiet rook move. The check looks strong but lets the king escape, while the rook move traps the king and mates on the next move. The lesson is that a move that attacks nothing can still win, and only the search sees it.

Figure 5 shows the tempting check beside the winning rook move. On the left the rook gives check up the file and the black king escapes through the green dots, while on the right the rook slides up the file to the third rank and traps the king, mating on the next move. Take the rook on e1: the check looks strong but lets the king escape, and the quiet rook move, which attacks nothing yet, wins.

Take a look at this tool. It runs the search on this chess position with different numbers of simulations and different amounts of exploring, and the move it picks changes with the settings. The lesson is that more simulations and the right amount of exploring make the search pick the winning move the network missed.
Try the tool. Press Play to run the search, and change the number of simulations and how much the search explores. Watch the move it picks change with the settings, and press Reset to start over.

Figure 6 shows the tool that runs the search on the position in Figure 2. The first guess here comes from a small hand-made stand-in, not the trained network. Take the simulations at few: the orange bar fills the whole track for the tempting check and the readout says the search keeps returning to the check it tried first.

Take a look at this figure. The network's first guess against the search's visits, once the search has run. The lesson is that the search moves the visits onto the winning rook move, while the network's first guess still favours the tempting check.

Figure 7 shows the search's visits beside the network's first guess, on the same chess position. Grey bars are the network's guess; orange bars are the search's visits. More simulations move the orange bars onto the winning rook move, while the grey bars favour the tempting check and the other rook moves. In the tool, with exploration at its lowest and Simulations on the stop labelled most, the tempting check stays the most visited single move, though the other rook moves together draw more visits.
Section seven, AlphaZero in practice

In every self-play game, each move runs one search. Replay keeps a memory of past steps, and training draws random batches from it. Here the replay memory, or buffer, holds positions from recent games. The network trains on them continually, and the newest network always plays.
AlphaGo Zero only let a new network play once it had beaten the old one; AlphaZero drops that test. It carries one network and the game buffer; the rules are given.

For each game it stores every position with the search policy and the final result. During self-play it adds Dirichlet noise at the root, a little random push to the prior there, so self-play tries moves the network would skip. During self-play it also draws moves in proportion to their visit shares to keep games varied, with temperature tau at 1 for the first 30 moves and then 0; in matches it plays the most visited move.
More simulations per move give stronger moves for more computing per move.

The games ran on Google's tensor processing units (TPUs), chips built for neural-network math. Self-play and training ran on separate sets of these chips. Training chess took 9 hours and 44 million self-play games, with each move searched by 800 simulations taking about 40 milliseconds; the replay window holds positions from the last 1,000,000 games, each position 119 planes of 8 by 8. The chip counts and training times follow the 2017 preprint; the 1,000,000-game replay window follows the Science 2018 version, which trained on 16 second-generation TPUs. A widely used reimplementation of the paper is AlphaZero General, a PyTorch version of the same loop.
7.1 AlphaZero’s settings

This table lines up the nine settings that trained AlphaZero, with the number each one takes. Read across a row to see one setting and its value, and down the Raise and Lower columns to compare the trade-offs. Simulations per move is 800: raising it gives stronger moves at more computing per move, while lowering it gives weaker moves at less computing per move. Training steps is 700,000: raising it gives a stronger network at more computing overall, while lowering it gives a weaker network at less computing overall. Minibatch is 4,096 positions per step: raising it gives steadier updates at more memory per update, while lowering it gives noisier updates at less memory per update. Learning rate starts at 0.2 and drops three times during training, to 0.02, then 0.002, then 0.0002: raising it gives bigger steps and faster learning that can overshoot, while lowering it gives smaller steps and slower learning that settles more surely. The PUCT bonus weight, c sub puct, is 1.25 at a fresh node and grows slowly as the parent is visited more: the card shows the simpler constant form, while the paper's weight grows by a log schedule with a starting weight of 1.25 and a base of 19652. A higher c sub puct leans more on the network's move chances and spreads visits over more moves, while a lower one sticks with the moves the search so far rates best. The L2 weight, c sub L 2, is 0.0001: a higher weight pulls every weight toward zero harder, so the network stays smaller but can underfit, while a lower one lets weights grow freer, so the network can fit more but can overfit recent games. The compute is 5,000 first-generation TPUs generating games and 64 second-generation TPUs training: more hardware means more games and faster training, while less means fewer games and slower training. Root noise, alpha, is 0.3 for chess, 0.15 for shogi and 0.03 for Go, blended into the prior with weight 0.25: more noise means a bigger random push at the root and more varied self-play, while less means self-play stays closer to the network's guesses. Self-play temperature, tau, is 1 for the first 30 moves and then 0: raising it gives more varied openings and slower settling on the best move, while lowering it means games follow the search sooner with less varied openings. The pattern is that the settings split into three groups: how hard the search works, how the model learns, and how much compute the training takes.

Table 1 lists AlphaZero's settings and what changing each one does. Each row names one setting, its value, what raising it does and what lowering it does, so a row reads as a trade rather than a fact. Take the simulations per move: raising them gives stronger moves at more computing per move, while lowering them gives weaker moves at less computing.
Section eight, Games with known rules
AlphaZero fits two-player games with a perfect, cheap simulator and a short list of moves.
It does not fit when the rules are unknown, or when actions are amounts such as a joint's turning force.
Dyna-Q spends its computing between the moves it really makes, to learn from fewer of them; AlphaZero spends it at every decision to choose a better move.
Section nine, Thin searches and repeated games

This table lines up four ways the search goes wrong, what causes each one, what it looks like, and what fixes it. Read across a row to see one failure, its cause, its symptom and its fix, and down the rows to compare the failures. Too few simulations is when the search barely moves off the prior: it plays like the network's guess and misses wins a few moves deep; the fix is more simulations, or a stronger network. Self-play falls into one way of starting the game is when the search always plays the most visited move: games repeat, and the network never sees other continuations; the fix is root Dirichlet noise and drawing self-play moves in proportion to their visit shares, keeping the most visited move for matches. The value head overfits recent games is when positions from one game are highly alike: value estimates swing between versions; the fix is to sample positions from many games in the buffer, and keep the L2 penalty term that pulls every weight toward zero. The wrong sign in the backup is when each edge is credited with the value as seen by the other player: the search steers toward moves that help the opponent; the fix is to flip the value before each edge update. The pattern is that every failure has a visible symptom and a concrete fix, and the fixes are to search more, to vary the starts, to learn from more games at once, or to flip the sign.

Table 2 lists how AlphaZero fails and what fixes each failure. Each row names one failure, its cause, what it looks like, and the fix, so a row reads as a diagnosis rather than a list of facts. Take the wrong sign in the backup: the search steers toward moves that help the opponent, and the fix is to flip the value before each edge update.
